entry: Russian polymath, scientist and writer. Among his discoveries were the atmosphere of Venus, the [[Conservation of mass|law of conservation of mass]] in [[Chemical reaction|chemical reactions]], and the theoretical prediction of [[Antarctica]]. One of the founders of modern geology, he also worked in natural science, chemistry, physics, [[Mineralogy|mineralogy]], history, art and philology. He became the first native full member of the Academy of Sciences in 1745. He studied under the philosopher Christian Wolff in Germany. He wrote odes and other poetry, and he influenced the formation of the modern Russian literary language. In 1755 he co-initiated [[Moscow State University]], writing its statutes and early curricula.

Russian novelist and winner of the 1965 [[Nobel Prize]] in Literature. He fought for the Bolsheviks in the Russian Civil War as a teenager and wrote about the [[Cossacks|Don Cossacks]] during the Russian Revolution, the civil war and collectivization. His major work, *And Quiet Flows the Don*, took him fourteen years to complete (1926–1940) and earned him the 1941 State Stalin Prize. Its authorship has been disputed since [[Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn]] claimed in 1974 that large portions were taken from the anti-Bolshevik Cossack writer Fyodor Kryukov. His novel *Virgin Soil Upturned*, which earned a Lenin Prize, reflects collectivization in the Don area.

Supersonic Soviet jet fighter and interceptor aircraft. Designed by the Mikoyan-Gurevich Design Bureau, its Ye-4 prototype first flew on 16 June 1955. It was the first successful Soviet aircraft combining fighter and interceptor roles, reaching Mach 2 with a relatively low-powered afterburning turbojet. Over 11,000 units were produced, and approximately 60 countries have flown it. Its nicknames include "Balalaika" and "Én Bạc", Vietnamese for "[[Swallow|silver swallow]]".

Large Soviet helicopter gunship and low-capacity troop transport. Introduced by the Soviet Air Force in 1972 and produced by the Mil Moscow Helicopter Plant, it is known to [[NATO]] as the Hind. Soviet pilots called it the "flying tank", and its cabin could hold eight passengers. Export versions, the Mi-25 and Mi-35, are denoted "Hind D" and "Hind E" in NATO circles. The helicopter is used by 52 countries. Unofficial nicknames included "Crocodile", for its camouflage, and "Drinking Glass", for the flat glass plates around the cockpits of earlier variants.

Family of medium twin-turbine transport [[Helicopter|helicopters]]. Designed by the Soviet Central Aerohydrodynamic Institute (TsAGI) and introduced into the Soviet Air Force in 1968, it is known to NATO as the Hip. The Mi-8 is the world's most-produced helicopter, with over 17,000 units used by over 50 countries. It is also used as an airborne command post, armed gunship and reconnaissance platform. [[Nikita Khrushchev]] reportedly ordered a similar helicopter after being extremely impressed by a U.S. presidential helicopter in 1959.

City (pop., 2026: 1,362,863), capital of Lombardy, northern Italy. It is Italy's second-largest city after [[Rome]] and its economic capital. Its metropolitan area, with about 6.55 million people, is the largest in Italy and the fourth-largest in the [[European Union]]. Founded by a Celtic tribe around 590 BC and conquered by the Romans in 222 BC, it served as capital of the western Roman Empire from AD 284 to 402. In the Late Medieval period the wealthy Duchy of Milan was one of the greatest forces behind the [[Renaissance]]. From the 19th century it led Italy's industrial and financial development. Its business district hosts Borsa Italiana, Italy's main stock exchange, and the city is a major center of fashion, design and tourism. It is home to AC Milan and Inter Milan, and its museums include major works by [[Leonardo da Vinci]].

Long-term climate cycles caused by variations in Earth's orbit and tilt. They are named after the Serbian geophysicist and astronomer Milutin Milanković, who in the 1920s gave a more quantitative analysis of James Croll's earlier hypothesis. Changes in orbital eccentricity, [[Axial tilt|axial tilt]] (obliquity) and precession alter the amount and location of solar radiation reaching Earth. Milanković emphasized changes at 65° north, where large land masses respond more quickly to forcing than oceans. The cycles help pace Earth's climate oscillations, including glacial and interglacial periods.

Unit of length in the British imperial and U.S. customary systems, equal to 5,280 feet or 1,760 yards. The statute mile was standardized by a 1959 international agreement between the [[Commonwealth of Nations]] and the United States that defined the yard as 0.9144 m, making the mile exactly 1,609.344 m (1.609344 km). For everyday use, 5 miles is roughly 8 km. The word derives from the Roman mile, or *mille passus* ("thousand paces"), which was about 1.48 km. The statute mile was made equal to 8 furlongs in 1593. The U.S. survey mile, based on the survey foot, was officially phased out in 2022. The [[Nautical mile|nautical mile]], now exactly 1.852 km, is used for maritime and aviation purposes.

American trumpeter, bandleader and composer. Davis was at the forefront of major developments in [[Jazz|jazz]], including bebop, cool jazz, hard bop, modal jazz, avant-garde jazz and jazz fusion. He made his professional debut in the bebop quintet of saxophonist [[Charlie Parker]] from 1944 to 1948. He led a sextet in the early 1960s with [[John Coltrane]], and *Kind of Blue* (1959) sold more than five million copies in the U.S. alone and 6.4 million copies worldwide. His million-selling *Bitches Brew* (1970) helped spark a resurgence in jazz fusion. After a five-year retirement due to poor health, he returned in the 1980s with pop-influenced albums. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2006.

American singer, songwriter and actress. She became a teen idol as Miley Stewart in the [[Disney Channel]] series *Hannah Montana* (2006–2011), and her album *Meet Miley Cyrus* (2007) reached number one in the U.S. Her 2013 album *Bangerz* produced "Wrecking Ball", which reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100. Her album *Endless Summer Vacation* (2023) spawned "Flowers", the best-selling single of 2023, which won two [[Grammy Awards]], including Record of the Year. She has also appeared in films such as *Bolt* (2008) and *The Last Song* (2010).

Series of [[Social psychology|social psychology]] experiments on obedience to authority, conducted at [[Yale University]]. Stanley Milgram tested whether participants would obey an experimenter who instructed them to give what they believed were electric shocks to a "learner", increasing to levels that would have been fatal had they been real. In the first version, every participant went up to 300 volts, and 65% went up to the full 450 volts. The experiments began three months after the trial of Adolf Eichmann started in Jerusalem, and Milgram sought to explain genocide and the claim that perpetrators were only following orders. Its applicability to the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]] is disputed.

National belief in a strong military capability and its aggressive use to expand national interests and values. The term may also imply glorification of the military and the "predominance of the armed forces in the administration or policy of the state." In Germany its roots lie in 18th- and 19th-century [[Prussia]]. [[Frederick William I of Prussia]] began large-scale military reforms in 1713, raising annual military spending to 73% of the Prussian budget. By his death in 1740 the army had 83,000 men, one of the largest standing armies in Europe. Because officers also furnished most civil officials, the army's interests came to be seen as the country's interests. [[Wilhelm II]] dismissed [[Otto von Bismarck]] in 1890. After World War I the [[Treaty of Versailles]] aimed to crush German militarism, which the Allies saw as a major cause of the Great War.

Fixed-wing or rotary-wing aircraft operated by a military force. Combat aircraft, such as [[Fighter aircraft|fighters]] and [[Bomber|bombers]], are designed to destroy enemy equipment or personnel with their own ordnance. Non-combat aircraft, such as transports and tankers, mainly serve support roles, though they may carry weapons for self-defense. Balloons were used for observation from 1794, when the French Aerostatic Corps flew one at the Battle of Fleurus, and they continued in the [[Napoleonic Wars]]. In 1909 the U.S. Army bought the [[Wright Flyer|Wright Military Flyer]]. Airplanes flew air combat and strategic bombing missions in [[World War I]], and in [[World War II]] early jet aircraft flew combat missions. In the [[Cold War]] era, jets exceeded Mach 2 and armament shifted mainly to missiles. Stealth aircraft entered development in the 1970s and saw combat in the 1980s.

Military regime in Brazil, 1964–1985. It was established on April 1, 1964, after a coup by the Brazilian Armed Forces, with U.S. support, against President João Goulart. Its guidelines were [[Nationalism|nationalism]], economic development and anti-communism. The regime practiced extensive censorship and human rights abuses, including institutionalized torture, particularly after the Institutional Act No. 5 of 1968. It is estimated that 434 people were killed or disappeared and 20,000 were tortured; some activists assert the figure is higher, but the armed forces dispute this. Brazil's regime provided a model for other military governments in [[Latin America]]. A new constitution in 1988 restored democracy.

Process of establishing and improving the capabilities of [[Military|military]] personnel in their roles. Training may be voluntary or compulsory, and in some countries it forms part of compulsory education. It begins with recruit training, which uses conditioning techniques to resocialize trainees so that they obey all orders without hesitation, and teaches basic military skills. Role-specific training follows, including the use of specialist equipment, and personnel may continue training throughout their careers. Drill instructors have the task of making service members fit for military use. Participants also learn survival skills such as cooperation and resilience. Directing staff are the military personnel who make up the instructional staff of a training institution.

Art, science and practice of designing and building military works and maintaining military transport and communication lines. Military engineers are also responsible for [[Logistics|logistics]] behind military tactics, and the discipline is a predecessor of [[Civil engineering]]. The word "engineer" was first used in warfare around c. 1380 to mean "a constructor of military engines". The Romans had a dedicated corps of military engineers, the architecti, who built a double wall of fortifications 30 miles (48 km) long to encircle Alesia in just six weeks in 52 BC. [[Vitruvius]] is the best known of these Roman army engineers. Military engineers also built siege machines such as [[Catapult|catapults]] and [[Battering ram|battering rams]]. In modern armies, soldiers trained to work under fire are called combat engineers.

Employment of military resources in training for military operations. Exercises test tactics and strategies without actual combat and ensure the combat readiness of forces before deployment. War games differ mainly in that they do not involve actual military forces; they use artificial players and models to consider multiple possible outcomes, not to predict results. Joint exercises involve several branches of one military, while combined, coalition, bilateral or multilateral exercises involve two or more countries. A 2021 study found that exercises within well-defined alliances usually deter adversaries, while exercises outside alliances, which are extremely rare, usually lead to conflict escalation. Exercises have sometimes served as cover for invasions, such as the [[Warsaw Pact]] invasion of Czechoslovakia and the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine.

Relationship between a country's military and the defense industry that supplies it, seen as a vested interest that influences public policy. Both sides benefit: one obtains weapons, and the other is paid to supply them. The concept is associated mainly with the United States. The phrase is often linked to [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]], whose January 17, 1961, farewell address warned against "unwarranted influence, whether sought or unsought" by the complex, although he was not the first to use it. The first known use was by Winfield W. Riefler in 1947. The phrase rose to prominence after the address, as part of opposition to the [[Vietnam War]]. The term has also been applied to Russia, especially since the beginning of the Russo-Ukrainian war.

Structuring of a state's armed forces to provide the military capability that national defense policy requires. Formal military organization tends to be hierarchical. In most countries the armed forces are divided into three branches: [[Army|army]], [[Navy|navy]] and [[Air force|air force]]. Some countries add cyber, medical, logistics, space or marine forces as independent services. Executive control is typically exercised by a ministry of defense, which in democracies is headed by an elected minister. The Roman Army used formal ranks, organized into legions of around 5,000 soldiers led by a legate and divided into centuries led by centurions. Most smaller countries have a single organization encompassing all their armed forces. Armies of developing countries tend to consist primarily of [[Infantry|infantry]], while developed countries' armies have larger units manning expensive equipment.

System of hierarchical relationships within armed forces, police and other institutions organized along military lines. Rank defines authority and responsibility within the chain of command, and it also sets pay grade, so that responsibility and pay rise together. Uniform insignia usually denote rank. Ranking systems have long helped logistics, command and coordination, and as operations grew larger, more ranks were created. Communist states have abolished ranks on several occasions, including the [[Red Army|Soviet Red Army]] from 1918 to 1935, but they re-established them after encountering operational difficulties. In Athens, ten generals (*strategoi*) were elected annually from 501 BC, one for each tribe; the position was an elected office rather than a military rank. The generals decided the battle plan at the [[Battle of Marathon]] in 490 BC by majority vote.

Units held back from battle so that they remain available for unforeseen situations or sudden opportunities. Reserves may defend against attack, be committed where the enemy exposes a vulnerability, or relieve troops already fighting. Their size depends on the commander's uncertainty about the enemy's intentions, a "hedge against uncertainty". Reserves exist at tactical, operational and strategic levels, and a reserve for one headquarters may not be one for a higher headquarters. The British Reserve Army of World War I was to carry out the breakthrough phase of the Somme offensive. The Reserve of the Supreme High Command was the principal reserve of the [[Red Army|Soviet Red Army]] in [[World War II]]; it is now part of the [[Russian Armed Forces]]. A military reserve differs from a military reserve force, a long-term part-time organization of reservists.

Study of military processes, institutions and behavior, and of the theory and application of organized coercive force. It focuses on the theory, method and practice of producing military capability consistent with national defense policy, and it identifies the strategic, political, economic and tactical elements that sustain military advantage. During the [[Industrial Revolution]] the term covered all matters of military theory and technology as a single academic discipline. In military education, departments with this name train junior officers rather than military scientists. Until the early 19th century, a British veteran of the [[Napoleonic Wars]] thought little had changed since the Greeks. Clausewitz argued that, unlike in other sciences or arts, "in war the object reacts." Operations research techniques pioneered in [[World War II]] optimized convoy routing and bombing patterns.

Set of ideas used by military organizations to pursue strategic goals. The term derives from the Greek *strategos*, and in the 18th century it was used narrowly for the "art of the general," or the arrangement of troops. [[Carl von Clausewitz]] defined military strategy as "the employment of battles to gain the end of war." B. H. Liddell Hart defined it as "the art of distributing and applying military means to fulfill the ends of policy," with less emphasis on battles. Strategy is broader than [[Military tactics|tactics]], which concern the disposition and maneuver of units on a battlefield. [[Sun Tzu]] is often considered the father of Eastern military strategy, which differs from the Western by focusing more on asymmetric warfare and deception. [[Chanakya]]'s *Arthashastra* has been an important compendium in Indian and Asian history.

Art of organizing and employing fighting forces on or near the battlefield. Tactics involve four battlefield functions: firepower, mobility, protection or security, and shock action. They are separate from command and control and from logistics, and they form the lowest of three levels of warfare, below the operational and strategic levels. Firepower advanced from melee weapons and bows to artillery, the rifled musket of the [[Crimean War]] and [[American Civil War]], and [[Machine gun|machine guns]] at the turn of the 20th century. For most of history, armies could not travel more than 32 km (20 mi) a day unless on rivers. Tanks in World War I improved mobility, and full tactical mobility was achieved in [[World War II]]. Field obstacles, often created by military engineers, can still limit tactical mobility.

Application of technology to warfare, comprising technology that is distinctly military in nature. Such technology usually lacks civilian uses or is dangerous without military training, though the line is porous, and civilian innovations have often been put to military use. Many new technologies arose from military funding of science. Armament engineering draws on mechanical, electrical, aerospace, materials and chemical engineering. Large-scale analyses of pre-industrial societies identify population growth, interregional connectivity, and enabling technologies such as iron and cavalry as major drivers of innovation. Humans in the [[Bronze Age]] learned to smelt copper with tin to make weapons. The [[Assyria|Assyrians]] are credited with introducing horse [[Cavalry|cavalry]] and extensive use of iron weapons by 1100 BCE. The [[Song dynasty]]'s *Wujing Zongyao* (*Essentials of the Military Arts*), written around 1043, covers strategy, training and advanced weaponry.
